chunks: Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Hammad ibn 'Uthman, who said:

I was present in the presence of Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) when a man said to him: 'May Allah improve you! You mentioned that Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him) used to wear coarse clothing, wearing a shirt for four dirhams, and something similar to that, and we see upon you good clothing.' So he (peace be upon him) said to him: 'Indeed, Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon him) wore that in an era where it was not disputed, and if he were to wear the like of that today, he would be known/defamed by it. So the best of clothing for every era is the clothing of its people, except that our Qaim (peace be upon him), when he rises, will wear the clothing of Ali (peace be upon him) and walk in his way.'

key_terms.الْخَشِنَ: Coarse or rough clothing, indicating simplicity and humility.
key_terms.الْقَمِيَةَ: A shirt or tunic, often used to denote simple, everyday attire.
key_terms.دَرَاهِمَ: Dirhams, a unit of silver currency used to indicate the low cost of the garment.
key_terms.سِيرَتِهِ: His way/methodology, referring to the practices and conduct of Ali ibn Abi Talib.
key_terms.قَائِمَنَا: Our Qaim (Riser), referring to Imam al-Mahdi (peace be upon him).
key_terms.لَشُهِرَ بِهِ: He would be known/defamed by it; becoming a subject of public attention or gossip due to its distinctiveness.

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on wearing simple versus expensive clothing according to the Imams?
ai.summary: This hadith illustrates the Shia jurisprudential principle of *al-mu'arafa* (social recognition) and contextual adaptation, where Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) distinguishes between the intrinsic virtue of simplicity and its social utility. He notes that while Ali ibn Abi Talib’s coarse dress was unremarkable in his era, wearing it later would cause *shuhrat* (prominence/distinction), potentially altering its spiritual message; thus, the ideal attire is that which blends with the local culture without ostentation. This principle is uniquely suspended for the Mahdi, who will deliberately adopt Ali’s specific dress to signal his identity and continuity with the Prophet’s household.

en.hubeali: Ahmad Bin Muhammad, from Muhammad Bin Yahya, from Hammad Bin Usman who said,

‘I was there in the presence of Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> when a man said to him<sup>asws</sup>, ‘May Allah<sup>azwj</sup> Keep you<sup>asws</sup> well! You<sup>asws</sup> mentioned that Ali<sup>asws</sup> Bin Abu Talib<sup>asws</sup> was wearing the coarse (clothes), wearing the shirt of four Dirhams, and what resembles that, and we see upon you<sup>asws</sup> the new clothes?’ So he<sup>asws</sup> said to him: ‘Ali<sup>asws</sup> Bin Abu Talib<sup>asws</sup> was wearing that during an era undeniably, and were he<sup>asws</sup> to wear the likes of that today he<sup>asws</sup> would have been defamed by it. So the best of the clothes during every era are clothes of its people, besides that when our<sup>asws</sup> Qaim<sup>asws</sup> rises, he<sup>asws</sup> would wear the clothes of Ali<sup>asws</sup>, and walk upon his<sup>asws</sup> way’.
en.sarwar: 15. Ahmad ibn Muhammad has narrated from Muhammad ibn Yahya from Hammad ibn ‘Uthaman who has said the following:

“Once I was with abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, when a man said, ‘I pray to Allah to keep you well, you have mentioned that Ali ibn abu Talib wore very rough-textured clothes. He wore a shirt valued at four dirham and similar items and we see you wear fine clothes.’ Abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, said to him, ‘Ali ibn abu Talib wore that kind of clothes in a time when it was not disliked. Were he to wear such clothes today he would have been defamed. The best dress in every period of time is what the people of that time use, however, when our al-Qa’im will rise, he will wear the kind of dress Ali, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, wore and follow his way of life.’”
